A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures, and image-based study examples, support reliable comparison after matching relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAE monosemanticity and reconstruction experiments, iNaturalist hierarchy analysis, concept-uniqueness analysis, and LLaVA steering results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and additionally reports human judgments of monosemanticity and concept-suppression examples.

M1.justification: The evaluated SAE architectures, MS computation, and intervention rule remain unchanged. Concept suppression uses negative values already permitted by v1's intervention parameter in Equation (10). The background ReLU loss correction does not establish a change to the evaluated methods.

E1.justification: v2 adds a human image-set comparison task involving Mechanical Turk annotators and concept-suppression scenarios involving knives and laptops. ImageNet and iNaturalist coverage is retained; the hierarchy experiment moves to Appendix E.3 rather than being removed.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain BatchTopK, Matryoshka BatchTopK, original neurons without SAEs, and unsteered LLaVA. Both CLIP and DINOv2 scoring encoders and the SigLIP experiments already appeared in v1. No new competing SAE or steering method is evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 16-image comparison grids, three judgments per pair, score-gap balancing, and human-agreement metrics, plus suppression tests at intervention values -5 and -20. DINOv2 becomes the default scoring encoder, including for hierarchy and sparsity analyses. The SigLIP extrema-table encoder label changes from CLIP ViT-L to ViT-B; unchanged values do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: The new user study tests whether MS agrees with human perception across score gaps and two scoring encoders. v2 also adds knife/laptop suppression case studies and DINOv2-based sensitivity and qualitative analyses. Existing hierarchy, reconstruction tradeoff, and Jaccard concept-uniqueness analyses remain present.

E5.justification: v2 adds majority-vote aggregation of three judgments per neuron pair and reports binned and cumulative human-alignment estimates with bin sample counts. Existing across-neuron standard deviations and steering uncertainty reporting remain unchanged. No new training-seed analysis, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds human-alignment results, including 79.0% agreement reported in Section 4.2.1, and suppression outputs in Figure 7. Hierarchy and sparsity MS results are replaced under the changed scoring encoder, so their numerical differences are not same-setting performance changes. Most matched tables remain identical, including quantitative steering results. One same-setting correction changes Matryoshka layer-17, expansion-8 worst MS from -0.08 to -0.09 in v1 Table A4 versus v2 Table A5.

T1.justification: Equation (3) changes the background ReLU reconstruction term from the Euclidean norm to its square. Appendix C also formalizes human/MS decisions and their alignment score. The central MS and intervention definitions remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions now claim human validation and introduce a benchmark derived from that study. Steering claims expand from inserting concepts to inserting or suppressing them. Hierarchical alignment loses its prominence as a headline contribution, although the underlying analysis remains in the appendix.

C2.justification: v2 explains that relative monosemanticity improves up to approximately expansion factor 4 and then declines, distinguishing this from increasing absolute neuron counts. It adds interpretations of human agreement and suppression as potential content filtering, plus an explicit limitation concerning untested alternatives to SAE dictionary learning.

D1.justification: v2 newly states project-code availability, specifies a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, and documents study neuron selection, annotator participation, payment, and question examples. Appendix D specifies three planned benchmark CSV files, including activations for 50,000 validation images. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the benchmark release remains prospective.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to COSMOS, FLAIR, BiomedGPT, and two audio applications while retaining the earlier SAE literature. Its comparison with concurrent multimodal monosemanticity research now emphasizes activation-aware, human-validated neuron-level scoring. The overall research positioning remains recognizable.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around human validation and steering. Hierarchy analysis moves from Section 4.3 to Appendix E.3, title-generation discussion moves to Appendix B, and the appendices gain a contents page and a more detailed subsection structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. Figure 1 is rearranged horizontally, qualitative grids are revised, and the main comparison table displays maxima only while full extrema remain in the appendix. New study plots, screenshots, and suppression figures accompany merged sensitivity panels and relocated existing displays.

improvement.justification: The human study substantially strengthens the central metric's evidential basis by directly testing agreement with human judgments, which v1 supported mainly through qualitative examples and indirect analyses. Suppression examples and expanded reproducibility documentation add further value. A material reporting inconsistency remains: Section 4.2.1 gives 93.5% agreement for score gaps of 0.8–0.9, whereas Table A1(a) gives 100%. This limits confidence in the exact rates, but both presentations support strong agreement at large gaps, leaving a substantial overall improvement.
